# What Is a Buying Committee?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A buying committee, also called a buying group or buying centre, is everyone at a customer who takes part in a purchase decision. Academic work since the 1960s and recent analyst surveys agree it is larger and more conflicted than sellers assume: Forrester found 13 people on average in 2024. For a commercial team the practical step is to record the committee on each opportunity, by role, and to sell to its consensus.

A buying committee is the group of people at a customer organisation who take part in deciding a business-to-business purchase: those who use, evaluate, fund, approve and contract for it. Researchers call it the buying centre; Gartner and Forrester call it the buying group. Recent surveys put it at 5 to 16 people, and conflict within it is common.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a buying committee means

Few B2B purchases are made by one person. A software tool is used by one team, assessed by IT, paid from another budget, reviewed by legal and approved by an executive. Any of them can stop it.

The concept comes from organisational buying research. Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind's 1972 paper in the *Journal of Marketing* modelled industrial buying as "an organizational decision-making process". It set out a concept of roles within the buying centre that later researchers extended. In 1982 Wind and Robertson proposed a sixth, "pin" role to manage interaction inside and outside the group. Wesley Johnston and Thomas Bonoma's 1981 study in the same journal measured real buying centres across 31 firms and 62 purchases, using 241 interviews.

"Buying centre" is the academic term, "buying group" the analysts' and "buying committee" the sellers'. They describe the same thing, though a formal committee is only one form it takes.

## How large it is

| Source | Year | Finding | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Johnston and Bonoma, *Journal of Marketing* | 1981 | Size grows with purchase importance, complexity and formalisation; services involve fewer people than capital equipment | 31 firms, 62 purchases |
| Gartner, buyer enablement research | Undated | Typical group of six to ten stakeholders | More than 250 B2B customers |
| Forrester, State of Business Buying | 2024 | 13 people on average; 89% of purchases involve two or more departments | Not stated in the release |
| Gartner, sales survey | 2025 | 5 to 16 people across up to four functions | 632 B2B buyers |

Samples and definitions differ, but the direction is consistent: more people than a seller usually meets, from more than one department.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

**Consensus is the hard part.** Gartner's May 2025 release defines unhealthy conflict as members having "conflicting objectives", disagreeing on the best course of action, or being overruled by external decision-makers. It found that content tailored to the group's shared needs improved consensus by 20%, while content focused only on individual relevance reduced it by 59%. Messaging each person separately can pull the group apart, which is the argument of [Positioning for Complex Markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/): give each role a reason to agree to one position.

**Single-threaded deals are fragile.** A deal with one engaged contact depends on that person's influence and tenure. [Revenue intelligence](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-intelligence/) tools flag it as a risk.

**Scoring should follow the group.** The case for scoring accounts rather than individual leads is set out in [Lead Scoring vs Account Scoring](https://lowob.com/research/lead-scoring-vs-account-scoring/).

In **lowob**'s model the committee is data in the store, attached to the opportunity as contact roles. Who approved, who objected hardest and who was never reached also feed win-loss reviews and the deal's decision record.

## How to map a buying committee

An illustrative role map for a mid-size services purchase. Role names vary by framework; [MEDDICC](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-meddicc/), for example, names an economic buyer and a champion.

| Role | What they care about | What to record in the CRM | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Economic buyer | Return and risk to the budget | Name, confirmed budget, decision date | Never met by the seller |
| Champion | Solving the problem they own | Name, the case they will make internally | Champion cannot name the approver |
| User lead | Daily workload and fit | Name, requirements raised | No user has seen the solution |
| Technical or IT reviewer | Security, integration, data | Name, review status | Review not started inside the quarter |
| Procurement | Terms, price, supplier risk | Name, process and timeline | Process discovered at the last minute |
| Legal | Liability and contract terms | Name, redline status | Redlines arrive after the close date |

Ask early who else will be involved, and record every answer as a contact role. Build a [mutual action plan](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/) with a named buyer owner for each step. At each pipeline meeting, check which roles are empty on late-stage deals. Agents can draft role-specific follow-ups, but each goes to the account owner before sending, because a message to the wrong member can undo a champion's work.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume a group.** Most B2B purchases involve people from more than one department.
- **Sell to agreement.** Consensus predicts deal quality better than any one person's enthusiasm.
- **Record roles on the opportunity.** Empty roles on late-stage deals are a forecast risk.
- **Score the account, not the lead.** One contact's activity says little about the committee.

## Common questions

### Who is on a B2B buying committee?

Typically an economic buyer, a champion, users, technical reviewers, procurement and legal. The mix depends on the purchase.

### How many people are on a buying committee?

Forrester's 2024 research found 13 on average. Gartner's 2025 survey found 5 to 16 people across up to four functions.

### What is the difference between a buying committee and a buying centre?

None in substance. Buying centre is the academic term from organisational buying research; buying committee and buying group are the sales and analyst terms.
